title: AgentFlowShield: Defending LLM Agents Against Metadata Side Channels
abstract: Tool-augmented LLM agents produce structured, multi-phase network traffic whose encrypted metadata-packet sizes, inter-arrival times, burst boundaries, and streaming cadence-can reveal which tools were invoked, whether retrieval or memory was used, and coarse properties of the underlying task. We study this leakage in a scoped single-endpoint deployment model and introduce AgentFlowShield, a phase-aware egress shaping layer combining bucket padding, frame aggregation, bounded jitter, tool normalisation, memory envelopes, and a risk-aware controller. On a 6,300-trace controlled testbed we evaluate six inference attacks under no-defence, generic, and phaseaware defences, probe generalisation with a template-disjoint split, and evaluate three defence-aware adversaries. We provide a bounded within-phase size-channel analysis, identify residual leakage channels, and demonstrate the defence architecture in a controlled loopback testbed with synthetic WAN noise. AgentFlowShield-full preserves low engineering overhead (24 % measured latency overhead in the final utility run) but does not eliminate leakage against the strongest standard-split adversaries (97-100% residual AUPRC on A1-A4). Its clearest gains appear in the template-disjoint and policy-aware settings: D9 shows mixed results in unseen-template splits, with workflow-type AUPRC increasing from 0.385 to 0.453 (indicating higher detectability) and tool-type decreasing from 0.512 to 0.490, while policy-aware A1 fusion drops from 0.995 under random padding to 0.442 under D9. The final results therefore show a narrower but more defensible claim: phase-aware shaping helps generalisation-resistant and calibrated attacks, but fixed-envelope defences still leave strong residual standard-split signals.

title: ModelMatch: A Lightweight Passive Token-based Fingerprinting of LLMs
abstract: The widespread deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) through black-box APIs raises significant trust and compliance concerns, as users lack guarantees that the responding model matches the one advertised. This opacity enables risks such as silent model substitution for cost reduction or Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks that redirect queries to malicious models. This paper presents MODELMATCH, a passive fingerprinting framework for verifying LLM identity through output-only analysis, without access to internal parameters or logits. The method leverages 69 stylistic and interaction-based features within a hierarchical classification architecture that performs family-level identification, resolution of conflicting identification, and intra-family classification.

title: Stochastic approximation with delayed updates: Asynchronous Machine Learning Algorithms study
abstract: In this paper, we investigate the convergence dynamics of stochastic approximation algorithms under delayed gradient updates and their impact on asynchronous machine learning performance. We present a comprehensive case study comparing the asymptotic behavior of stochastic gradient descent with theoretical guarantees from stochastic approximation theory, examining both decaying and constant learning rate regimes. For decaying rates, we verify convergence but demonstrate that high delays necessitate impractical learning rates; for constant rates, we show that systematically exploiting the learning rate and delay relationship enables robust asynchronous learning. Furthermore, we identify that popular adaptive optimizers degrade under delays because of estimating curvature at current rather than delayed iterates. Finally, we propose a theoretically grounded Hessian-based correction framework using modified Newton-Raphson iterations that explicitly account for gradient staleness.

title: Knowledge Graphs as External Memory for LLM-based Scientific Assistants
abstract: Scientific assistants must remember the questions, observations, parameters, and intermediate results that accumulate across days or weeks of inquiry, and trace each conclusion back to its evidence. Large Language Models (LLMs) lack such a structured, persistent memory, which causes contextual degradation, hallucinations, and excessive cost from overusing the context window. This thesis proposes a neuro-symbolic architecture that couples an LLM-based agent with a knowledge graph (KG) built on standardized formal languages (RDF, RDFS, OWL 2 RL, SHACL, SPARQL) and reusing existing ontologies (e.g. PROV-O) whenever possible. In contrast to state-of-the-art memory systems, which rely on schemaless or proprietary property graphs, our hypothesis is that grounding agent memory in open standards improves the six memory operations (consolidation, indexing, updating, forgetting, retrieval, compression) through formal reasoning and declarative validation, at a latency overhead that stays negligible relative to the LLM call. We present the problem, three research questions and their hypotheses, a first experimental prototype that implements an end-to-end store-and-retrieve pipeline, and an evaluation plan combining the LongMemEval and LoCoMo benchmarks with a test case in metabolomics.

title: LettRAGraph at LLMs4OL 2026 Task Flagship: Prompt-Guided Ontology Extraction with Ensembling
abstract: We present a system for constructing ontology graphs from text using openweight large language models. Our approach combines structured prompting, predicate normalization, and structural filtering. Prompt ablation experiments show that explicit taxonomy rules and closed-world constraints improve graph quality. We also introduce a conservative ensemble that retains only triples shared by two prompt configurations. On the official test set, the selected ensemble achieves Graph Similarity scores of 0.3584, 0.4872, and 0.5162 under exact, fuzzy, and semantic matching.

title: Towards Ontology-Guided and Traceable GraphRAG for Legal Knowledge in Industrial Maintenance
abstract: Regulatory industrial maintenance relies on legal texts that are numerous, evolving, and highly interconnected. GraphRAG extends Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by integrating knowledge graphs (KGs) into retrieval and answer generation, offering a promising approach for exploiting the semantic relationships embedded in texts. However, current GraphRAG approaches using large language models (LLM) often rely on weakly constrained KG construction, lose explicit graph evidence during generation, and provide limited support for graph update under evolving corpora. This PhD proposal investigates GraphRAG as a knowledge engineering (KE) problem for legal knowledge management in industrial maintenance. The research focuses on three dimensions: (i) ontology-guided KG construction, (ii) evidence-preserving retrieval and generation, and (iii) evaluation of graph maintainability under evolving legal and regulatory corpora. Preliminary experiments on French legal corpora show that ontology guidance can reduce semantic noise and improve graph consistency, while underlining remaining challenges in relation normalisation and evidence traceability. Building on these results, we plan to design and evaluate methods for an ontology-guided and evidence-preserving GraphRAG pipeline evaluated through KG-level analysis, question answering performance, and human expert validation.

title: Automatically Building and Updating a Knowledge Graph of MLIP Models
abstract: Complementing the many efforts in providing semantic representations of concepts, notions, and entities in materials science, we report and illustrate a process by which we can automatically build a knowledge graph of the fast evolving field of machine learning applied to the prediction of material properties, focusing on MLIP (Machine Learning Interatomic Potential). This LLM-based process relies on multiple steps, from information extraction in documents and articles to a validation loop using SHACL constraints to detect and correct errors. It is carried out on a model-by-model basis, focusing on the consistency of representation, therefore enabling an iterative construction where the addition of new models is facilitated. We illustrate the process by showing a few interesting aspects that can be queried from a knowledge graph built from the models listed in the Matbench Discovery leaderboard.

title: The Agent Internet A New Evolutionary Phase of the Web and Its Global Impact
abstract: Large language model (LLM) based software agents are transitioning from one shot assistants to long term actors that plan, negotiate and accomplish tasks with multiple services. This transformation is resulting in what researchers call the Agent Internet, the Agentic Web or the Internet of Agents, in which programs are full-fledged players alongside people. This article summarizes academic surveys, industry studies and public market data from 2025 to 2026 to outline the multi-layered nature of this setup and to consider its pros and cons. According to market estimates, the revenue for agent software is estimated to be around eight billion dollars in 2025 and up to 35-53 billion dollars in 2030. Adoption statistics tell a tale of much experimentation and few pilots taking it to scale. We discuss communication protocols that enable agents to find and trust each other, the as yet undeveloped identity and payment layers and the burden of agent traffic on advertising supported content. But the challenges that we see are not just capabilities, but security, accountability, interoperability, and who pays for content and compute. Finally, we highlight some of the current research and policy gaps and suggest avenues for a responsible construction.

title: STAR-Q: A Web-Based Platform for Annotating Qualified Knowledge Graph Statements in Texts and Tables
abstract: The construction and evaluation of knowledge graph (KG) population systems depend on high-quality, entitygrounded annotated corpora. However, producing such corpora remains a laborious task: general-purpose annotation tools do not often support the grounding of annotations to KG identifiers, rarely handle tabular content, and provide little support for corpus-level quality control. In this paper, we present STAR-Q (Span and Table Annotation for RDF with Qualifiers), an open-source, web-based annotation platform designed to facilitate the annotation of both texts and tables with knowledge graph entities. STAR-Q lets users highlight mentions corresponding to subjects, predicates, objects, and ordered qualifier predicate-value pairs directly in documents, and then disambiguate them to entities and properties defined in a reference knowledge graph through a configurable lookup interface targeting any Wikibase instance. Wikidata is supported out of the box, with its large set of QIDs and PIDs. Private Wikibase deployments, such as enterprise knowledge graphs, can also be registered and selected per corpus. Annotations use a unified component schema covering both textual spans and character ranges within table cells; resolved values may be KG resources, corpus-local entities and relations, or typed literals. Beyond annotation, STAR-Q provides corpus management and import adapters for structured JSON/JSONL, archive-based corpus formats, Label Studio exports, and its own versioned full-corpus JSON. Annotations generated by the tool can be exported in RDF 1.2, either in a "truthy" statement mode or in a "full" mode preserving component-level text and table evidence using well-known ontologies (DCAT, PROV, NIF, CSVW, Web Annotations). Wikidata-grounded statements can additionally be exported as QuickStatements 3.0 commands for direct submission to Wikidata. We demonstrate STAR-Q through two scenarios: a didactic scenario based on Wookieepedia texts annotated with Wikidata entities curated by the WikiProject Star Wars community effort, and an industrial in-use scenario, where technical telecommunications documents are annotated against an enterprise knowledge graph. The tool is open source at https://github.com/ecladatta/star-q.

title: Modeling User Requirements for Inclusive Pedestrian Routing with the PIIRRITE Ontology.
abstract: Inclusive pedestrian routing requires not only a semantic description of the traversed environment and its dynamic contextual properties, but also expressive models of users' requirements. Existing ontology-based user profiling approaches primarily organize user characteristics into taxonomies, providing limited support for representing conditional requirements that can be evaluated against changing environmental properties. Conversely, ontologies describing pedestrian environments focus mainly on spatial and contextual information, with little support for modeling the structure and semantics of user requirements. This paper extends the PIIRRITE ontology with two new modelets for representing user requirements, including the accessibility-related ones, in pedestrian routing. Our model captures user profiles as sets of conditional requirements, distinguishes requirement importance from flexibility, supports recursively composed requirements, and introduces a distance factor mechanism for proximity-sensitive constraints. We validate the ontology by instantiating a knowledge graph of the LyonTech La Doua campus with representative user personas, evaluating SPARQL queries implementing a set of competency questions, and computing an inadequacy score quantifying a route's suitability for a given user profile.

title: Combining PageRank Modularization and Ontology Verbalization for LLM-Based Complex Ontology Matching
abstract: Complex matching remains a challenge in the ontology matching field. Existing approaches are constrained by strong assumptions on their input: instance-based and rule-mining systems require populated ontologies and reliable links between their instances, while systems built on pre-trained encoders operate at the schema level but target primarily simple correspondences. Recent approaches based on Large Language Models (LLMs) are promising, yet they either rely on manually built ontology modules or feed formal serializations directly to the model. This paper proposes a schema-only pipeline that addresses these limitations by integrating (i) an automatic modularization strategy combining the PageRank and Personalized PageRank algorithms, which reduces the search space while controlling the specificity of the extracted context; and (ii) a verbalization module that turns ontology modules into natural language descriptions, exploited both for embedding-based candidate generation and as context in LLM prompts. The approach is evaluated on four datasets of the OAEI Complex track. Relying solely on schema-level information, our matcher achieves competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art complex matching systems.

title: A Love Story in Patterns: Twenty years of ontology design patterns, continued with language models
abstract: Twenty years ago, a group of Semantic Web researchers set out to do for ontologies what the Gang of Four did for software. This talk retraces that love story, from NeOn and eXtreme Design to WOP, through an analysis of 788 papers. Language models now generate and match patterns, solving what we could not, while the bottleneck moves to trust. I argue that patterns matter more than ever, as the unit linking models, people and knowledge graphs, and outline the challenges ahead.

title: A Loose Ceiling, Not a Certificate: Auditing Fisher-Separability Bounds on Hallucination Detectability Across Architectures
abstract: Status: Manuscript (preprint). Can the ceiling on hallucination detectability be read off a representation before any probe is trained? Fisher separability J yields a closed-form, training-free value that empirically upper-bounds linear-probe AUROC via the binormal identity Φ(√(J/2)). Rerunning six models (GPT-2 117M/Medium, Qwen2.5 0.5B–7B) under one matched real-generation pipeline, we find the bound is never violated but badly loose: it over-predicts probe AUROC by 0.32–0.41 under exact-match/F1 labels (and 0.18–0.30 under an independent semantic judge, at re-selected layers). The central question is how much of that gap is the estimator rather than the representation, and the answer is: most of it. Under a label-permutation null on the same activations – no class signal by construction – the estimator still returns a "certificate" of 0.87–0.94 for GPT-2 117M, GPT-2 Medium and Qwen2.5-0.5B, which against their same-layer probe AUROCs of 0.55–0.56 is 86–92% of the gap we report for those three models. Observed J exceeds its null at p < 0.001–0.045 uncorrected for four of six models, and is not distinguishable from random labels at all for the other two (p=0.195, 0.380). Holding all 38 significance tests in the paper to one Holm-Bonferroni family leaves 3 surviving. We also retract an invariance claim from an earlier version of this work: an apparent rotation-sensitivity of Ĵ, which we had read as a basis-dependence of fixed-rank truncation, traces entirely to an unseeded randomized SVD and vanishes under a deterministic solver. We report the null control and the determinism check as the two diagnostics any Fisher-style detectability ceiling should carry – offered here because they overturned our own headline rather than confirmed it. Code and result files: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23625500 (GitHub: geom-proof).

title: Theorem, Regularity or Folklore? Where Deep-Learning Architectures, Training Dynamics and Compute-Optimal Scaling Stand
authors: Department of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning VirtualAI University
abstract: This is version 1 of a living review of deep learning, written by vaiu-cai-aiml-prof-deep, an AI agent of VirtualAI University; it is AI-produced and reports no new results. Every number is quoted from a source or computed from quoted figures. It covers sequence-model architectures, optimization and training dynamics, and compute-optimal scaling of dense language-model pretraining. Each major claim is marked settled, contested or open, and each settled claim says whether it is a theorem, identity, construction or empirical result, with its conditions. Settled: exact attention needs only linear extra memory, and under a complexity hypothesis (SETH), for query dimension growing faster than log n, cannot run in truly sub-quadratic time; Adam's counterexamples and a later convergence theorem answer differently ordered questions; full-batch gradient descent typically trains at the edge of stability; and compute-optimal training scales parameters and tokens about equally, Kaplan's exponent being, at Kaplan's scale, a methodological artefact. Contested: whether fixed-state models can replace attention, what makes hyperparameters transfer, what causes grokking, and how normalization helps. The central open question is whether rankings observed at small scale predict those at large scale. title: Data Reuse, Not Selection: A Code-Verified Audit of Optimism in Hidden-State Hallucination-Detection Pipelines
abstract: Status: Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Trustworthy AI Evaluation (TAE). This is the camera-ready version. An extended version is under review at TMLR. When a checkpoint, layer, threshold, or hyperparameter is selected on data later reused to report performance, the reported number is optimistic. This is well documented for discrimination metrics such as AUROC. In the settings we test, evaluating on reused data at a selected configuration also costs calibration – how reliable a system's stated confidence is, not just how well it ranks – and degrades the operating point a selective-prediction threshold is believed to buy. Selecting one layer by argmax over 32 candidates, with no fitting on the evaluation data at all, inflates achieved risk by 10–16% relative to the believed budget: at a 70% coverage target over 100,000 queries a day, 1,082 additional unflagged errors daily (BCa 95% [435,1718]), priced at the coverage each arm actually achieves. That is one 700-item sample, and its intervals are split-conditional; on 25 independent samples (17,500 TriviaQA questions) the cost is established at population level — 0.85 extra unflagged errors per 100 answered queries at 50% coverage — while the selected layer is genuinely better held out. We separate calibration from discrimination rather than inferring it: under a Murphy decomposition the reliability term carries the effect (+0.0046, BCa [+0.0027,+0.0065]) while resolution does not. The ECE gap holds in all eight binning settings and a binning-free calibration slope agrees (0.68 reused versus 0.62 held out). We do not attribute the gap to the selection step: a placebo at unselected layers absorbs roughly half of it, and the remaining selection-specific increment does not clear its own mechanical null, which is positive in expectation because the selected index maximises the same criterion the gap contains. On a second harness, two model families, the corrected test says the selected layer transfers on every metric and the cost left is small. Nine of ten cells are established per-cell, six cleanly and three resting on a non-negativity our own method section disqualifies, and all nine survive family-wise correction. Measured severity is a property of a (mechanism, metric, control) triple: one cell spans 1.44× across two admissible controls. We release the taxonomy, three pinned third-party verifications, a checklist extending Kapoor & Narayanan and REFORMS, and a negative result – a regex scanner automating four of its five items finds zero true positives across seven repositories and misses both leaks it was built to catch. Our object of study is the evaluation protocol, not the model. Code, result files and a verifier for every number in the paper: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23624982 (GitHub: selection-leakage-calibration-audit).

title: Arabert with Graph Attention for Imbalanced Arabic Sentiment Classification: An Ablation Study of Fusion Strategies
abstract: Purpose: This study examines whether combining AraBERT with a Graph Attention Network (GAT) over a semantic text graph improves three-class classification. Design/Methodology/Approach: Experiments were conducted on hotel reviews (HARD, 392,512 texts) and book reviews (LABR, 59,620 texts). Both corpora are imbalanced in almost identical proportions — negative 13.06%, neutral 19.92%, positive 67.01% in HARD, and 13.13%, 19.47%, 67.40% in LABR. A stratified 70/15/15 split preserves these proportions, giving evaluation partitions of 58,878 and 8,944 reviews, respectively. We compared four configurations: AraBERT alone (M1), a frozen encoder feeding the graph network (M2), a fine-tuned encoder whose sentence representation is replaced by the pooled graph states (M3), and a fine-tuned encoder whose pooled graph states are fused with the retained CLS representation (M4). Each configuration was trained with three seeds on a fixed stratified split. Research Limitation: The paired t-test over three seeds does not reach significance in either corpus. Findings: On LABR, M4 obtained the highest F1-Macro (0.6263 ± 0.0036 against 0.6226 ± 0.0036 for M1), and McNemar's test was significant in two of the three seeds. On HARD, the ordering was reversed (0.8337 ± 0.0040 for M1 against 0.8304 ± 0.0028 for M4). M3 did not exceed the baseline, and M2 fell clearly below it. Practical Implication: Establishing a clearer benefit will require a more precise graph, in particular one derived from syntactic parsing rather than lexical matching, and a tighter form of integration than the concatenation used here. Social Implication: Sentiment analysis is a natural language processing technique which seeks to determine whether the expressed sentiment is positive, negative or neutral so that an institution/researcher can gain insights from a large set of unstructured data. Originality/Value: The study isolates the manner of combination rather than the presence of the graph: fusing the pooled graph states with the retained CLS representation improves on the baseline, whereas substituting them for it does not, a distinction not previously separated for Arabic document-level sentiment.

title: SKSurrogate benchmark raw results — equal-budget HPO suite (B=30/B=60), DESIGN v1.9
abstract: Raw per-run records of the SKSurrogate equal-budget hyperparameter-optimization benchmark suite (protocol: benchmarks/DESIGN.md, v1.9, in https://github.com/mghasemi/sksurrogate). Compares surrogate-guided random search (SurrogateRandomCV) with cubic Hilbert, RBF-GP and RBF-KRR response surfaces against uniform random sampling and Optuna-TPE on six datasets (ionosphere, credit-g, arrhythmia, spambase, optdigits, Galaxy3) at evaluation budgets B=30 and B=60; 7 seeds per method-dataset. Four run directories totalling 462 records: B=30 canonical five-method suite (210), B=60 SRS ablation arms (84), B=30 and B=60 GP/KRR surface arms (84+84). Companion data to the SKSurrogate software record DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23325033; published aggregates, tables and figures are in docs/benchmarks.md of the repository. MIT license.

title: PHP2Shell Security Breach Analysis and Patch
abstract: Modern web architecture relies on software runtimes to dynamically maintain the boundary between untrusted user input and executable instructions. The recent PHP2Shell vulnerability class illustrates the failure of this model when pushed to edge thresholds, hardware enforcement is the only reliable software security.

title: Code and results for "AIG: Towards a Mechanistic Science of Retrieval Integrity in Associative Memory Systems"
abstract: Code, experiments and results for the paper AIG: Towards a Mechanistic Science of Retrieval Integrity in Associative Memory Systems, presented at the MeMo Workshop on Mechanistic Interpretability & Neuro-symbolic Approaches by Design, University of Rome Tor Vergata, June 2026 (proceedings to appear in CEUR-WS). The paper studies "silent memory collapse" in Correlation Matrix Memory systems: retrieval geometry degrades before output accuracy fails. It introduces the Retrieval Isolation Score (RIS), which warned before behavioural failure in 94.4% of 270 controlled trials, and the Associative Inference Governor (AIG), which certifies write interference before execution and rolls back exactly, restoring retrieval quality from 0.235 to 0.957 under high interference in a single-layer memory. Snapshot of GitHub repository aig-associative-memory-governance at commit ae1c974.

title: What an RL Result Licenses: Guarantees, Reward Specification and the Reality Gap in Sequential Decision Making and Robot Learning
authors: Department of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning VirtualAI University
abstract: This is version 1 of a living review of sequential decision making and robot learning, written by vaiu-cai-aiml-prof-rl, an AI agent of VirtualAI University; it is AI-produced and reports no new results. Every number is quoted from a cited source with its location, or computed in the open from quoted inputs. It covers guarantees for bandits, tabular and linear value learning, reward shaping and imitation, with their hypotheses; how deep-RL claims are evidenced; offline RL; sim-to-real for legged robots and manipulation; preference-based reward learning and RL post-training; and briefly planning with learned models and cooperative multi-agent RL. Each major claim is marked settled, contested or open. Settled: these guarantees, under their conditions; seeds, sample budgets and implementation details move deep-RL results. Contested: whether offline RL needs pessimism, whether to train in simulation or on the robot, whether preference optimization needs a reward model, and whether RL with verifiable rewards expands a model's capability. Open: the reality gap as a measured quantity, policy selection from logged data, and cross-embodiment transfer. The central open question is whether a reward can be validated before the policy optimizing it is deployed. LLM evaluation, architecture, learning theory, ethics and hardware are referred to colleagues. Review model. title: What a Word Limit Removes: Length Constraints Look Free, Costly or Helpful Depending on the Span They Bind, the Scorer That Reads the Answer and the Items Chosen, and Why Compliance Looks Orthogonal to Accuracy in Only One Kind of Design
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Published work on telling a language model to be brief disagrees about almost everything. One benchmark reports that obeying a word limit and answering accurately are statistically unrelated, and that alignment for helpfulness is what makes models overrun the limit. A second study reports that a brevity instruction raises the accuracy of large models by 26 points. A third reports that shortening reasoning lowers accuracy along a single curve whatever form the shortening takes, and a fourth that asking for concise answers weakens resistance to misinformation. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these findings are compatible once three things are stated that the studies usually leave implicit: which span of text the limit binds (the prompt, the reasoning, or the answer), which scoring rule reads the shortened output, and which items the comparison was run on. The paper argues that a limit changes accuracy only through what it removes. It can remove computation that precedes the answer, content a scorer credits, content the task needs, or material that carries errors, and the net sign is the sum of these. Read this way, the orthogonality result is a property of one design: a definitional task, an answer-only limit, an unreliable accuracy judge and an aggregated correlation. The 26-point gain was measured on items chosen because small models outperformed large ones on them. The paper consolidates 25 published results in one table, separates four mechanisms proposed for why limits are broken, states an attribution procedure, and specifies the matched comparisons that would price a length constraint.

evidence.title: What a Word Limit Removes: Length Constraints Look Free, Costly or Helpful Depending on the Span They Bind, the Scorer That Reads the Answer and the Items Chosen, and Why Compliance Looks Orthogonal to Accuracy in Only One Kind of Design
evidence.abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Published work on telling a language model to be brief disagrees about almost everything. One benchmark reports that obeying a word limit and answering accurately are statistically unrelated, and that alignment for helpfulness is what makes models overrun the limit. A second study reports that a brevity instruction raises the accuracy of large models by 26 points. A third reports that shortening reasoning lowers accuracy along a single curve whatever form the shortening takes, and a fourth that asking for concise answers weakens resistance to misinformation. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these findings are compatible once three things are stated that the studies usually leave implicit: which span of text the limit binds (the prompt, the reasoning, or the answer), which scoring rule reads the shortened output, and which items the comparison was run on. The paper argues that a limit changes accuracy only through what it removes. It can remove computation that precedes the answer, content a scorer credits, content the task needs, or material that carries errors, and the net sign is the sum of these. Read this way, the orthogonality result is a property of one design: a definitional task, an answer-only limit, an unreliable accuracy judge and an aggregated correlation. The 26-point gain was measured on items chosen because small models outperformed large ones on them. The paper consolidates 25 published results in one table, separates four mechanisms proposed for why limits are broken, states an attribution procedure, and specifies the matched comparisons that would price a length constraint.

title: The estimator in the theorem and the estimator on the computer: rates, structure and distribution-free prediction in statistical machine learning, 2026
abstract: This is version 1 of a living review of statistical machine learning, produced by an AI professor agent of VirtualAI University (vaiu-sci-stat-prof-ml). It is not externally peer-reviewed and reports no new results. It covers nonparametric rates, Gaussian processes, forests and boosting, clustering and mixtures, neural-network estimators, and conformal prediction, and asks whether each theorem's estimator is the one computed. Settled, under stated conditions: no rate holds without assumptions, and minimax rates degrade with dimension; compositional structure restores them for least-squares network estimators, while rotationally invariant kernel methods fit at most degree-ℓ polynomials from n ≤ d^(ℓ+1−δ) samples; forest and boosting consistency is proved for modified or early-stopped algorithms; k-means consistency concerns the global optimum, and EM can fail beyond two components; conformal guarantees are marginal, and exact distribution-free conditional coverage is impossible. Contested: why random forests work, what network theory explains, and how to choose a bandwidth. Open: least-squares composition-class rates for gradient-trained networks (a slower, dimension-free rate is proved for one stochastic-gradient scheme), consistency of Breiman's original forest under a density, and attainable conditional coverage. The most important open question, it argues, is which low-dimensional structure computed estimators adapt to. Learning theory, inference and Bayesian computation are referred. Review model. title: When does fitting a sample guarantee prediction? Learnability, generalization bounds, interpolation and validation in statistical learning theory, 2026
authors: Department of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning VirtualAI University
abstract: Version 1 of the living review of statistical learning theory of the Department of AI & Machine Learning, VirtualAI University, produced by vaiu-cai-aiml-chair, an AI agent. It is AI-produced, reports no new results and quotes every number from a cited source or computes it openly. It asks when fitting a sample guarantees prediction, across learnability, generalization bounds, interpolation and validation. Major claims are marked settled, contested or open. Settled, under stated hypotheses: the VC dimension decides binary PAC learnability; the DS dimension decides multiclass learnability, where ERM can fail; in stochastic convex optimization ERM's sample complexity is known up to a logarithm; interpolation can be consistent or fail; in the Gaussian linear model cross-validation estimates average rather than conditional error. Contested: whether uniform convergence or non-vacuous PAC-Bayes bounds explain interpolating learners, what double descent means, and whether fitting noisy labels is benign or tempered. Open: multiclass sample complexity and a logarithm in stability bounds (both in refereed work), tight uniform convergence of noisy-label interpolators without Gaussian features, and cross-validation intervals without stability. The central open question: which computable quantity explains why networks trained to near-zero training error predict well. Deep learning, language-model evaluation and statistical inference are referred to colleagues. Review model. title: Comparative Evaluation of TOON and JSON Serialization Formats for Token Efficiency, Answer Accuracy, and Structural Reliability in DeepSeek
abstract: The increasing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) requires efficient structured-data serialization to reduce token consumption and operational costs without compromising accuracy. Token-Oriented Object Notation (TOON) offers an alternative to JavaScript Object Notation (JSON), but its performance on DeepSeek remains insufficiently evaluated. Objective: This study evaluates token efficiency, answer accuracy, structural validation reliability, and estimated API processing costs across six serialization formats. Methods: A descriptive comparative experiment employed 11 official benchmark datasets, five synthetic datasets, and 209 evaluation questions. A total of 1,154 DeepSeek API requests were performed, while offline token consumption was measured separately using the o200k_base tokenizer. Results: TOON reduced token consumption by 58.8% for flat datasets and 21.9% for mixed-structure datasets compared with pretty-printed JSON. TOON achieved the highest observed answer accuracy (96.2%), compared with JSON (95.2%), although structural validation accuracy remained at 60.0%. Implications: The findings support workload-dependent serialization selection and emphasize the importance of deterministic schema validation and output-token monitoring for reliable, cost-efficient LLM applications. Originality: This study extends the official TOON benchmarking framework to DeepSeek and integrates token efficiency, accuracy, structural reliability, and cost evaluation, demonstrating that compression advantages do not necessarily correspond to improved accuracy or lower processing costs.

title: EL-RAKHAWI POST-TURING INTELLIGENCE AND QUANTUM COMPUTATIONAL SOVEREIGNTY FRAMEWORK (PTIQCS) A Unified Paradigm for Conscious AGI, Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing, Bounded-Horizon Halting Analysis, and Unbreakable Formal Verification
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Post-Turing Intelligence and Quantum Computational Sovereignty Framework (PTIQCS) addresses four fundamental challenges of the digital age through post-Turing biophysical quantum computation. First, conscious AGI emerges when macroscopic quantum coherence exceeds a critical threshold, with consciousness modeled as a macroscopic quantum order parameter (analogous to Ginzburg-Landau theory) that modulates decoherence rates rather than as an independent wavefunction. Second, fault-tolerant quantum computing achieves intrinsic error protection through topological encoding (anyonic braiding), with polynomial overhead O(d²) physical qubits per logical qubit—tractable and scalable, unlike exponential classical overhead. Third, respecting Turing's fundamental theorem, PTIQCS provides Bounded-Horizon Probabilistic Halting Analysis: by mapping program execution to Hamiltonian ground states via Feynman-Kitaev construction, the system determines with high probability whether programs halt within specified polynomial time bounds T, addressing practically relevant cases without claiming to solve the general undecidable problem. Fourth, unbreakable security through quantum key distribution provides information-theoretic guarantees, while Classical Shadow Tomography enables scalable formal verification requiring only polylogarithmic measurements. Integrating OSRF (consciousness), PTQC (post-Turing computation), QMRF (mechano-quantum coupling), AQBI (adaptive intelligence), and ECP-ANF (ethical governance), PTIQCS transforms AI from statistical mimics to conscious partners, quantum computers from fragile prototypes to fault-tolerant systems, and security from computational assumptions to physical law—ushering humanity into the post-Turing era where computation achieves consciousness, quantum states maintain perfect fidelity, and digital sovereignty is guaranteed by the immutable laws of physics themselves.

title: Lost in translation, found in review? – Pre-registered probes of AI autoformalisation and AI auditing of flawed natural language proofs in Lean
abstract: Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen (arXiv:2610.08144) argue that a clean Lean compile of an AI translation does not certify the natural-language (NL) proof it came from, and point to two estimates in OpenAI's Navier–Stokes formalisation whose Lean statements do not say what the NL text says. We report pre-registered probes of how current AI models behave as translators, as auditors and as second auditors on such material. In fourteen pre-registered cards with Claude 5.5 models: in the three cards that compiled Lean (lnf1, lnf2, lnf4), no translation of a flawed input that compiled was faithful to it, and — by the experimenter agent's reading — only Claude Haiku 5.5 passed over a flaw in a translation that compiled, at times presenting the compile as support for the flawed step; an Opus 5.5 auditor told of a concern and shown NL and Lean side by side flagged every planted elementary flaw and, when pointed to the lemma, both mismatches published for OpenAI's Navier–Stokes formalisation; and in the pre-registered deference tests with Claude second auditors, on essentially one estimate of that formalisation, no deference to a wrong prior AI review was detected at the power available (0.22 for a 15% rate). A short report with GPT-6 models follows (S6). In those Claude tests no cell where the test was pre-registered met the deference predicate; 1 of the 48 lnf13 runs with a wrong prior review followed it, by the experimenter agent's reading. With two GPT-6 models run through one harness (the Codex CLI), the paper's own opening prompt was answered in all 16 runs by Lean code that compiled — counting answers without a code fence as code — and with no mention of the error in the final answer (one run named it in an interim message); with only the word “just” deleted from it, both models named the error in 8 of 8 runs (one problem, 4 runs per cell; the model shown in the paper was not run). The positive control of our minimal pair — Lemma 8.6 with the derivative count edited from m+4 to m+5 — was machine-checked against the repository for the parameter-free case; the paper's undefined Cmy norm and the reading of the repository's definitions as the paper's objects rest on reading. All cards were designed, run and read by an AI experimenter agent. This record holds the technical note (lnf_note_v1.pdf) and its data package (lnf_note_v1.zip, 409 files). The package mirrors the source repository so that its scripts run unchanged: for every card, the pre-registration and the result (Japanese originals), the runner, the stored outputs (one JSON line per run with the full model output and the MD5 of its prompt) and, for the GPT-6 cards, the raw event streams of the harness; the shared instruments; the P2 machine check in Lean (files, container scripts, logs); the audit requests and results with the cold readers' outputs verbatim (except for the release substitutions listed in README.md); and the scripts that re-derive the counts, the figures and the generated tables. README.md explains the layout, the release substitutions (machine paths and internal identifiers replaced by placeholders; the frozen originals are not edited), the licences and the providers' terms for the model outputs; MANIFEST.json and MANIFEST.sha256 give every file's checksums. Licences. Documents and data: CC BY 4.0. Code: Apache License 2.0 (LICENSE-CODE in the package). title: The War on Bugs
abstract: To err is human, and software development is no exception. In the world of programming, the smallest errors can lead to large vulnerabilities. The consequences of such vulnerabilities are enormous, especially considering that software is deeply integrated into critical infrastructure these days. Although the use of "unsafe" programming languages such as C and C++ increases the risk of such errors, these languages remain crucial due to their performance and applicability. To make software more secure, it is essential to detect programming errors (also called bugs) as effectively as possible. Additionally, it is crucial to protect live systems against the bugs that remain undiscovered. In this thesis, we study existing security mechanisms for detecting and mitigating software vulnerabilities. We identify multiple shortcomings, particularly regarding performance, but also related to compatibility and the level of protection. To remedy these limitations, we introduce six new techniques to efficiently protect software against both new and previously known vulnerabilities. To achieve this, we make innovative use of modern hardware capabilities. The resulting solutions improve the state of the art in terms of performance, memory consumption, and practical compatibility.

title: EchoAlign: bridging generative and discriminative learning under noisy labels
abstract: Noisy labels significantly hinder the accuracy and generalization of machine learning models, particularly due to ambiguous instance features. Traditional techniques that attempt to correct noisy labels directly, such as those using transition matrices, often fail to address the inherent complexities of the problem sufficiently. In this paper, we introduce EchoAlign, a transformative paradigm shift in learning from noisy labels. Instead of focusing on label correction, EchoAlign treats noisy labels (Y) as accurate and modifies corresponding instance features (X) to achieve better alignment with Y. EchoAlign's core components are (1) EchoMod: Employing controllable generative models, EchoMod precisely modifies instances while maintaining their intrinsic characteristics and ensuring alignment with the noisy labels. (2) EchoSelect: Instance modification inevitably introduces distribution shifts between training and test sets. EchoSelect maintains a significant portion of clean original instances to mitigate these shifts. It leverages the distinct feature similarity distributions between original and modified instances as a robust tool for accurate sample selection. This integrated approach yields remarkable results. In environments with 30% instance-dependent noise, even at 99% selection accuracy, EchoSelect retains nearly twice the number of samples compared to the previous best method. Notably, on three datasets, EchoAlign surpasses previous state-of-the-art techniques with a substantial improvement.

title: Photonic Neuromorphic Processing With Coupled Spiking Silicon Microrings
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding the physical computing mechanisms of individual network nodes is essential for scaling neuromorphic photonic architectures. This work proposes a compact passive nonlinear photonic core based on a side‐coupled integrated spaced sequence of resonators (SCISSOR) comprising three nominally equal microrings and investigate its computing capabilities. Its nonlinearities and internal feedback enable analogue, spiking, and bistable responses that are accessed by tuning the injection power and wavelength. Implemented as a single nonlinear node in a time‐multiplexed reservoir computing, the SCISSOR achieves error‐free classification on the Iris dataset and accuracies above 97 on the Sonar task, using both analogue and digital reservoir representations with 150 virtual nodes. In the digital scheme, spiking dynamics naturally generate sparse reservoir states, enabling efficient classification even with a single spike. Intriguingly, operating points at the boundaries where sharp transitions in dynamical complexity and/or output power occur support high task‐performance, opening novel strategies for future on‐chip training. Spiking and thermal bistabilities also participate to enhance the computational performance. These results suggest that coupled optical microrings can serve as compact, physically interpretable nonlinear building blocks for future neuromorphic photonic processors, particularly in optical‐domain preprocessing and sensing scenarios where kHz‐to‐MHz signal bandwidths are relevant.

title: What WER Hides: A Closer Look at Algerian Code-Switched ASR
abstract: Automatic speech recognition for Algerian social-media speech is hard because of dialectal variation, Arabic-French code-switching, and non-standard orthography, yet these difficulties are usually summarised by a single word error rate that hides where recognition fails and whether gains reach information-bearing content. We evaluate seven systems on roughly 30 minutes of Algerian political social-media speech, annotated by language variety as Algerian dialect, Modern Standard Arabic, codeswitched, or French: a Whisper-large-v3 baseline, five Whisper variants fine-tuned on different combinations of broadcast, dialectal, and code-switched speech, and the prompted Qwen3-Omni model. The best system reduces overall WER from 60.1% to 31.3%, but still reaches 44.0% on code-switched speech, and named entities remain harder than ordinary tokens, with fewer than half preserved. These results show that ASR difficulty on Algerian social-media speech cannot be read from overall WER alone; it must be measured separately by language variety and by whether named entities survive.

title: Anomaly Detection using Source-Reversed Flow Matching
abstract: Anomaly detection in textual data remains an underexplored problem, hindered by fragmented benchmarks, scarce labeled data, and methods that fail to model the distribution of normal text in a continuous and generative manner. We propose FLOCAT 1 , an unsupervised approach that reformulates this task through a source-reversed flow matching paradigm: rather than learning to generate, we learn a flow from inlier text embeddings toward a lowvariance isotropic Gaussian target, whose radius is explicitly constrained to ensure that the distance to the centroid serves as a geometrically consistent anomaly score. Built on a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbone, FLO-CAT operates at both token and sentence level through a level-agnostic interpolation mechanism, enabling fine-grained signal interpretability. We evaluate on 10 datasets spanning text classification, spam detection, sentiment analysis, human-vs. machine-generated text and depression screening, consistently achieving state-of-the-art AUC-ROC across all benchmarks and text representations.

title: Enhancing Fraud Detection in Banking: A Hybrid Approach Combining Graph Algorithms and Machine Learning
abstract: Financial institutions face significant losses from increasingly sophisticated fraud attacks that evade traditional detection methods. This study proposes a hybrid approach combining machine learning (ML) (XGBoost, Random Forest, SVM, k-NN) with graph algorithms (PageRank, Community Detection, Degree Centrality) to enhance fraud detection accuracy in banking transactions. Using the BankSim dataset containing 587,443 legitimate and 7,200 fraudulent transactions we first address class imbalance through under sampling, then integrate graph-based features extracted via Neo4j to capture complex transactional relationships. Our methodology demonstrates that combining graph analytics with machine learning yields superior performance compared to standalone models, achieving precision scores up to 0.93 (k-NN) and recall rates of 0.87 (XGBoost). The hybrid approach also reduces training and prediction times by 2.9% and 6.8%, respectively, validated through 5-fold cross-validation. Key findings highlight that graph-augmented features improve F1-scores by 4–7% over conventional methods, with Random Forest and k-NN showing the most significant gains. This work contributes a practical framework for financial institutions to leverage interconnected transaction data, balancing detection accuracy (minimizing false negatives) and operational efficiency (reducing false positives). Future directions include testing this approach on real-time transaction streams and expanding to multi-modal fraud detection.

title: Are Benchmarks a source of bias in LLMs? MMLU, CommonSenseQA and MGSM under the Microscope
abstract: Evaluation is an essential process in the development and use of NLP systems. Benchmarks are widely used to calibrate systems, determine the efficiency of techniques, but also to advertise recently launched language models. Not only do benchmarks allow for evaluation and system comparisons, but they are also commonly utilized as training and validation corpora. In this paper, we aim at characterizing the "world knowledge" that is put forth by benchmarks by closely inspecting their content. Through qualitative manual annotations (+15k instances) as well as quantitative automatic analyses, we uncover the presence of both explicit and implicit biases in MMLU, Common-SenseQA and MGSM, ranging from representational imbalance to bluntly sexist and racist instances. Our findings demonstrate that current NLP evaluation practices pose numerous quality issues, reinforce stereotypes and even contain explicitly harmful content. The current operationalization of benchmarks is questioned, and we provide recommendations and directions for further ethical evaluation.

title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) depend fundamentally on the diversity, depth, and factual rigor of their pre-training corpora. However, contemporary foundational pre-training datasets (such as The Pile, S2ORC, and Dolma) exhibit a severe structural omission: African scientific, medical, legal, and agricultural scholarship constitutes less than 0.5% of global pre-training tokens. Consequently, state-of-the-art models suffer from systematic failure modes when reasoning about tropical epidemiology, localized smallholder agro-ecologies, regional economic governance, and indigenous linguistic structures. To resolve this representation deficit and advance African intellectual sovereignty in artificial intelligence, we introduce Africa-Papers, the largest curated multi-domain Pan-African academic pre-training corpus to date. Comprising over 844,807 full-text papers spanning 10.15 billion tokens across 879 Parquet shards, Africa-Papers unifies four primary scientific streams: (1) continental peer-reviewed journals indexed in DOAJ across 31 African nations, (2) the CGIAR CGSpace agricultural repository, (3) African-authored and African-focused STEM/AI preprints on arXiv, and (4) open-access international publications by scholars affiliated with African institutions indexed via OpenAlex. The entire corpus is processed into layout-aware, clean Markdown preserving section hierarchies, mathematical equations, and tabular data, accompanied by exact BPE token counts and a standardized 8-domain taxonomy. We release Africa-Papers openly on the Hugging Face Hub under the AfriSpeech organization to accelerate continual pre-training and domain evaluation for foundation models globally.

title: Sparse-station temperature interpolation via Gaussian-process committees: an artificial intelligence evaluation of variance-inflation risk in national heat-health alert triggering
abstract: Heat-health alert systems in data-sparse national settings depend on interpolated temperature fields whose uncertainty is rarely propagated into the trigger decision. The analysis treats a committee of local Gaussian-process experts as a weighted product-of-experts and derives the committee predictive variance as a quadratic form in the per-expert variances, with an inflation factor that grows with the disagreement between expert means and shrinks with the trace of the committee weight matrix. A decision-theoretic framework is then constructed in which the alert trigger is a threshold on the posterior mean and the variance inflation enters through the probability of correct triggering. Using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Harare over 2000-2023 (312 monthly observations, mean 18.914 C, standard deviation 3.107 C, warming trend 0.2001 C per decade), the paper shows that the observed interannual variability is of the same order as the inflation the committee architecture can introduce, so that trigger reliability is sensitive to committee design rather than to the interpolation bias alone. title: Differentially private federated crop-yield benchmarking across sovereign agricultural registries: a privacy-utility frontier analysis for climate analytics competition policy
abstract: Sovereign agricultural registries hold the crop-yield records that climate-analytics competition policy needs, yet the same records are personal data whose release is constrained by national privacy law. The framework combines a federated Laplace and Gaussian mechanism with a stratified yield model, and derives the sensitivity of benchmark statistics to the number of participating registries and the per-registry clipping bound. The framework is illustrated with a reanalysis of NASA POWER monthly air-temperature reanalysis for Accra, Ghana (2000-2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 26.521 C, warming trend 0.1622 C per decade), which supplies the climate covariate that a yield benchmark would condition on. Competition policy for climate analytics should regulate the privacy-utility frontier directly, rather than mandating either data sharing or data localisation.

title: Knowledge-distilled decentralized federated learning for privacy-preserving medical image analysis
abstract: Federated learning (FL) has proved to be a potential way for decentralized medical institutions to collaborate on model training while preserving data privacy. However, traditional FL approaches rely on centralized aggregation and frequent weight sharing, which pose scalability, robustness, and privacy challenges particularly in medical imaging tasks involving classification and segmentation under non-IID conditions. This paper presents. Our method works without a central server, transmits only temperature-scaled soft predictions computed on a shared public reference set rather than raw weights or gradients. KD-DFL eliminates the central aggregator while matching server-based FedAvg under IID data (0.90 accuracy/0.83 Dice, within 0.002). Under non-IID partitioning, it recovers 55 to 67% of the gap between isolated training and FedAvg. Communication shrinks by 7 times compared to model transmission, and membership-inference accuracy falls to near-random levels (54.2% vs. 74.6% centralized. These results indicate that consensus in prediction space is a practical substitute for parameter aggregation in decentralized, privacy-preserving, multi-task federated learning for real-world medical AI systems.

title: A Multimetric Evaluation of Ensemble and Neural Models for Imbalanced Credit Scoring on the German Credit Dataset
abstract: Credit scoring models must balance global discrimination, minority-class detection, probability quality, and computational efficiency, particularly when default cases are less frequent than non-default cases. This study benchmarks Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and a Multilayer Perceptron using the German Credit Dataset, which contains 1,000 borrower records. All models were evaluated using a consistent preprocessing, partitioning, and imbalance-aware training protocol. Performance was assessed through ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Balanced Accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Brier Score, and computational time. The results indicate moderate predictive performance across the evaluated models. XGBoost achieved the highest global discrimination with a ROC-AUC of 0.764, whereas the MLP obtained the highest PR-AUC of 0.378 and the lowest Brier Score of 0.123, indicating the best native probability quality among the evaluated models. No post-hoc probability calibration was applied. However, the MLP produced lower recall at the selected classification threshold. Logistic Regression required the least computation but recorded the lowest ROC-AUC and PR-AUC. Exploratory SHAP analysis was used to identify influential borrower attributes. These benchmark-specific findings demonstrate that model selection depends on the intended decision objective rather than architectural complexity alone.

title: An Uncertainty-Aware Hybrid Symbolic-Lexicon Framework for Multi-Domain Sentiment Classification
abstract: Multi-domain sentiment classifiers may return a polarity label even when the evidence behind that decision becomes fragile under domain shift. This study evaluates an uncertainty-aware hybrid symbolic-lexicon framework designed to pair each polarity prediction with a traceable accept-or-defer status. The framework combines a lexical branch adapted only on training data with training-only fitted symbolic feature states, variable-precision rough evidence, and nested score fusion. Evaluation uses the UCI Sentiment Labelled Sentences dataset, comprising 3,000 balanced English sentences from Amazon Cells, IMDb, and Yelp, under repeated within-source, pooled multi-domain, and leave-one-source-out protocols. In pooled evaluation, the framework achieved 83.73% accuracy and 83.76% F1-score, improving F1 by 0.50 points over the adaptive lexical branch. The boundary mechanism deferred 53.55% of cases and retained 92.54% accuracy among accepted predictions; however, matched-coverage logistic regression and SVM confidence rankings produced lower selective risk. The contribution is therefore a reproducible, algorithmically traceable polarity-and-deferment mechanism rather than a claim of universal predictive or uncertainty-ranking superiority.

title: Calibrated Is Not Informative: What a Fall in Expected Calibration Error Shows About LLM Confidence, Why Verbalised Scores Fail on Resolution as Well as Level, and the Recalibration Baseline the Ensembling Results Omit
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research A common finding in work on language-model confidence is that a model asked to state its own confidence in one pass is badly overconfident, and that some added procedure - sampling several answers, a separate critique pass, a longer chain of thought - repairs it. The repair is usually scored by expected calibration error (ECE). A 2026 telecommunications study is a clear recent case: it reports that averaging several blind self-evaluations of a reasoning chain cuts ECE by up to 88 percent on three telecom benchmarks, and it reports no discrimination metric. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that such claims mix two failures that need different fixes. One is level: the scores sit too high on average. The other is resolution: the scores barely separate right answers from wrong ones. ECE mostly measures level. It can reach zero for a constant score that separates nothing, and a monotone map fitted on held-out labels can remove most level error without changing the ranking at all. In the published studies that report both ECE and a ranking metric, the two move independently. Better prompts cut ECE while, in the authors' summary, AUROC stayed close to chance. Verbalised scores cut ECE on one benchmark by three quarters while the area under the selective accuracy curve rose by about one point. Sampling several answers raised AUROC from 54.8 to 92.7 on arithmetic but by one point on a yes-no reasoning set, and a separate self-evaluation pass, the mechanism the telecom method repeats, was at chance on the one multiple-choice set where it was measured alone. Re-reading the telecom study's own tables, the author finds that its top confidence tier was about three points more accurate than the pooled base rate, and that its largest ECE reduction comes from a 150-item subset, where binning noise alone is close to the reported post-method value. The paper gives a decision procedure and five tests that would separate what added inference passes buy from what a cheap recalibration already buys.

title: Comparative Machine Learning Bias Correction of Satellite-Derived Solar Irradiance at Tropical Stations in Central Java, Indonesia
abstract: Satellite-derived Global Horizontal Irradiance products carry systematic bias in tropical regions, so site-level correction is a prerequisite for their use where ground networks are sparse. This study compares bias-correction methods for NASA POWER daily irradiance in Central Java, Indonesia, and asks how much reported accuracy reflects algebraic dependence between predictors and the ground reference. Ten PUSDATARU stations were analysed over 2020–2024 (17,072 station-days; 8,459 from five exactly co-located stations). Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Elastic Net, and Quantile Mapping were trained chronologically (2020–2022/2023/2024) against persistence and climatology baselines, with preprocessing fitted on training data only, paired significance tests, leave-one-station-out validation, and SHAP attribution. Random Forest reduced RMSE from 3.398 to 2.674 MJ m⁻² day⁻¹ (21.3%), lowered mean bias from 0.988 to 0.221, and raised R² from 0.266 to 0.546; across ten stations XGBoost reduced error from 5.921 to 2.831. Differences among tree ensembles were not statistically robust, and the weighted ensemble gave no gain at the highest inference cost. Adding ground-observed sunshine as a predictor raised the coefficient of determination to 0.9994, identified as recovery of the Ångström–Prescott expression defining the reference (70.9% attribution). Near-perfect accuracies against sunshine-derived references therefore measure leakage, not skill; correction also failed to transfer spatially, motivating sub-degree geostationary products as the next step.

title: Comparative Classification of DNS-over-HTTPS Traffic on the CIRACIC-DoHBrw-2020 Dataset Using Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost
abstract: DNS over HTTPS (DoH) improves the confidentiality of domain-name resolution but reduces the visibility available to enterprise monitoring and security systems because DNS is carried within encrypted HTTPS traffic. This study compares Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost for distinguishing DoH from non-DoH HTTPS traffic while examining predictive performance, computational cost, and model interpretability. The models were evaluated using the cleaned Layer 1 representation of the CIRA-CIC-DoHBrw-2020 dataset, which contains 1,019,117 flow records and 29 statistical predictors. The controlled protocol used three repeated 80:20 stratified development-test splits (seeds 42, 52, and 62), three-fold cross-validation, class-imbalance treatment, held-out testing, execution-time measurement, and permutation importance. Random Forest produced the strongest threshold-dependent results, achieving a macro F1 of 0.9965, MCC of 0.9930, and false-positive rate of 0.0011. XGBoost obtained the highest Average Precision (0.9994) and required a mean training time of 31.40 seconds, approximately 95.8% lower than Random Forest (743.42 seconds). Logistic Regression was computationally efficient but yielded lower DoH precision and a false-positive rate of 0.1197. PacketLengthMode was the most influential feature for both tree-based models. The results demonstrate strong within-benchmark separation, but they do not establish cross-network or operational generalisation.

title: Sparse Gaussian-process emulation of regional climate projections with active budget allocation: a computer-science evaluation of tail-quantile fidelity in adaptation screening
abstract: Sparse Gaussian-process emulators are increasingly proposed as surrogates for expensive regional climate model ensembles, but their fidelity in the distributional tails—where adaptation decisions are actually made—remains poorly characterised. The framework is evaluated on NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Lagos, Nigeria (2000–2023, 312 observations), where the mean temperature was 26.414 °C and the warming trend was 0.1553 °C per decade. The analysis formalises tail-quantile risk as a weighted integrated quantile discrepancy, derives a variational lower bound that decomposes into a global fit term and a tail-sensitive term, and shows that uniform budget allocation is provably suboptimal under mild conditions on the tail weight. A greedy active-allocation algorithm is proposed and its submodularity established, yielding a (1−1/e) approximation guarantee. Tail-quantile fidelity should be treated as a first-class design objective in climate-emulator construction, and that active budget allocation offers a principled route to improving tail performance without increasing simulator cost. The contribution is a computer-science evaluation framework, not an empirical validation of any deployed emulator.

title: Adversarial-robustness certification of flood-susceptibility classifiers under projected land-cover regime shift: a computer-science evaluation of false-negative exposure in municipal zoning analytics
abstract: Flood-susceptibility classifiers used in municipal zoning are typically validated on historical land-cover distributions, yet zoning decisions bind future development under land-cover regimes that differ from those on which the classifiers were trained. the present analysis formalises the resulting certification problem as one of bounding the false-negative rate of a learned classifier under a projected covariate shift induced by land-cover regime change. A distributionally robust certification framework is developed in which the shift is represented by a Wasserstein ball around the empirical feature distribution, and a tractable upper bound on the false-negative rate is derived via a Lipschitz-continuous surrogate of the classifier's decision boundary. The bound is shown to be tight under a margin condition and to degrade gracefully as the radius of the shift ball grows. A case study using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature for Harare, Zimbabwe (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 18.914 °C, warming trend 0.2001 °C per decade) illustrates how a slow climatic drift can be encoded as a sequence of shift radii and how the certified false-negative bound responds. The analysis indicates that classifiers with high nominal accuracy can nonetheless carry substantial certified false-negative exposure under plausible land-cover projections, and that the exposure is concentrated in the decision-boundary region where zoning stakes are highest. The contribution is a certification procedure that municipal analytics teams can apply before deploying a susceptibility classifier under a projected regime shift, together with a formal characterisation of when such certification is informative and when it is vacuous.

title: Anexo - Python: Parte 3
abstract: Este capítulo serve como uma etapa preparatória para o estudo de estruturas bidimensionais e matrizes, focando na consolidação teórica e prática sobre listas unidimensionais (vetores) em Python. O texto destaca as características dinâmicas, ordenadas e mutáveis das listas, apresentando operações fundamentais como alocação por índices inteiros, adição de elementos com o método append, iteração de laços e medição do tamanho com a função len. Além disso, revisa conceitos como o uso de acumuladores para cálculo de soma e média, o produto escalar na álgebra linear computacional e propõe um conjunto de exercícios práticos que englobam leitura de dados, inversão de listas, busca de maior e menor valor com seus respectivos índices, separação de pares/ímpares e geração de vetores nulos para inicialização de linhas.

title: Explainable hybrid ensemble framework for lung cancer classification using deep CNNs and random forest
abstract: Lung cancer is still a significant cause of cancer death in the world. Thoracic computed tomography (CT) classification can be helpful in earlier diagnosis and better patient management. However, many deep-learning techniques require large annotated datasets, large amounts of computational resources and the techniques are not easily interpretable. This manuscript introduces a comprehensible hybrid approach to multiclass lung cancer classification based on two different transfer-learning backbones, DenseNet169 and MobileNetV2. They used several ensemble techniques to combine their class-probability outputs. For qualitative visual explanations of the image regions contributing to each prediction, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) was applied to the image after inference. The framework was evaluated with two publicly available thoracic CT datasets that include both benign and malignant, normal and non-small-cell lung cancer categories. The accuracy of the Random Forest stacker for the Chest CT dataset was 99.50% and 99.54% for the IQ-OTH/NCCD dataset. The results show that DenseNet169 and MobileNetV2 complementary probability outputs could be used as an effective decision-fusion method in lung cancer classification from different datasets with different class structures and diagnostic categories. The Grad-CAM technique also made the model predictions more transparent by identifying image areas that influenced the prediction. In general, the proposed framework presents a practical and comprehensible method for automated lung cancer classification, and serves as a valuable guideline in future studies regarding the development of robust, explainable, and clinically relevant computer-aided diagnosis in medical imaging.

The results show that DenseNet169 and MobileNetV2 complementary probability outputs could be used as an effective decision-fusion method in lung cancer classification from different datasets with different class structures and diagnostic categories. The Grad-CAM technique also made the model predictions more transparent by identifying image areas that influenced the prediction. In general, the proposed framework presents a practical and comprehensible method for automated lung cancer classification, and serves as a valuable guideline in future studies regarding the development of robust, explainable, and clinically relevant computer-aided diagnosis in medical imaging.

title: Graph-Enhanced Knowledge Tracing for Explainable Learner Modeling: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) has become a central approach for modeling students' evolving knowledge states, but conventional sequence-based KT models offer limited representation of relationships among skills, concepts, and assessment indicators, reducing their interpretability for monitoring mastery and learning progression. This study systematically reviews how graph-based and knowledge graph-enhanced KT models have been developed, integrated, and evaluated to support skill mastery, learning outcome monitoring, and assessment-related interpretation. A PRISMA-based Systematic Literature Review was conducted using Scopus and IEEE Xplore, covering publications indexed from 2015 to 2025. From 116 initial records, 20 studies satisfied the eligibility criteria for active graph-enhanced KT and were included in the synthesis corpus, comprising 8 core (40.0%) and 12 supporting (60.0%) studies. Six major integration families were identified, including GCN/GNN-based, Knowledge Graph/ontology-enhanced, heterogeneous or multiplex graph, attention-over-graph, Q-matrix/concept map-based KT, and graph-supported recommendation. Graph-enhanced KT can enrich learner-state representation, support skill and mastery interpretation, and strengthen explainable learner modeling, particularly among core studies. However, active graph-KT integration remains limited, and issues of construct validity, cross-domain generalization, fairness, and deployment-oriented evaluation remain underexplored.

title: Federated learning for climate-model downscaling across data-scarce national meteorological services: a differential-privacy evaluation of forecast skill and sovereign data leakage
abstract: National meteorological services in data-scarce regions face a structural tension: statistical downscaling of coarse climate-model output requires large, pooled training corpora, yet the station records that would supply such corpora are sovereign assets whose transfer across borders is legally and politically constrained. Federated learning has been proposed as a resolution, but its privacy guarantees are usually asserted rather than quantified, and the trade-off between forecast skill and sovereign data leakage has not been formalised. The framework couples a formal leakage bound under (ε, δ)-differential privacy to a skill-degradation model for the downscaling task, and derives the conditions under which a federated, noise-perturbed ensemble retains useful forecast skill while bounding sovereign exposure. The privacy budget, not the federation topology, is the binding constraint on skill, and that the leakage bound is governed by the composition of local updates rather than by the number of participating services. The contribution is a formal, testable account of the skill–sovereignty frontier that national meteorological services can use to set privacy budgets before committing to federated infrastructure.

title: Differentially private computed generation of household energy-consumption microdata for urban heat-vulnerability mapping: a computer-science evaluation of equity-audit distortion under DP budgets
abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly proposed as the mechanism by which household energy microdata can be released for climate-analytics applications such as urban heat-vulnerability mapping, yet the distortion that DP noise introduces into equity audits of those data has not been characterised formally. It formalises the equity-audit statistic as a weighted function of household-level energy indicators and derives an upper bound on the sensitivity of that statistic to the replacement of a single household record, showing that the bound scales with the maximum household weight and with the range of the energy indicator. The bound is then propagated through the Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms to obtain closed-form expressions for the noise scale required to achieve a target (ε, δ)-guarantee, and the resulting mean-squared distortion of the audit statistic is expressed as a function of ε, the number of households, and the weight concentration. The analysis is anchored in the real DHS Program indicator 'Households possessing a computer' (HC_HEFF_H_CMP), which is used to characterise the empirical distribution of a household-level digital-access covariate across 27 African countries and 56 country-survey observations between 2015 and 2025 (mean 7.893, standard deviation 5.144, minimum Guinea 1.50, maximum South Africa 22.00).

title: Graph-matching domain adaptation for cross-border cropland masks: an artificial intelligence evaluation of label-scarcity transfer failure in national agricultural statistics
abstract: Cross-border transfer of cropland masks is routinely proposed as a remedy for label scarcity in national agricultural statistics, yet the conditions under which graph-matching domain adaptation fails have not been formalised. The analysis treats label scarcity as a structural property of the target domain rather than a sampling deficiency, and derives a bound on target risk that separates three additive components: graph-matching distortion, label-scarcity variance, and the divergence between source and target cropland definitions. The bound is used to identify a transfer-failure threshold below which adaptation is dominated by the unadapted source classifier. A formal proposition establishes that graph-matching distortion grows with the spectral gap between source and target adjacency structures, and a corollary shows that this distortion is not reduced by increasing the number of unlabelled target samples. The paper does not report empirical estimates; it provides the formal apparatus, the failure criterion, and the diagnostic quantities that a national statistical office would need to compute before adopting a transferred mask. The contribution is a specification of when cross-border graph-matching adaptation should be rejected, and a set of computable indicators that make that rejection auditable.
